data.title: Crop insurance claims set for multi-year high as weather losses mount
data.description:
Crop insurance claims for the Kharif 2026 season are expected to exceed premiums collected, with insurers anticipating this to be one of the worst ever periods in the sector due to prolonged dry spells, uneven rainfall, and cyclonic activity that hit agricultural production across several states.
 
The industry's loss ratio — which measures claims as a proportion of premiums — is expected to be well above 100 per cent, making the current Kharif season one of the most challenging for crop insurers in the past eight to nine years, according to early industry estimates. However, they expect the claims picture to become clearer by the end of November or early December.
 
According to insurance brokers, the season could be comparable to 2015-16, when India experienced a super El Niño and the agriculture sector experienced severe losses, following which the government launched a crop insurance scheme named 'Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY)'.
 
“(The) Industry is expecting losses worth thousands of crore in crop insurance this time, while the premiums charged were nearly 50 per cent less than last year due to better claims experience in the previous season,” an insurer said.
 
Prolonged dry spells during August and September, particularly in rain-deficient regions, have affected crop production across several key states. Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Karnataka, and Madhya Pradesh are among the major states facing the impact of El Niño conditions, while Haryana and Andhra Pradesh are also likely to see elevated claims.
 
The low rainfall situation has added to the pressure, with several agricultural regions across Punjab, Haryana, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Assam and the Northeast experiencing varying degrees of moisture stress. October's cyclonic activity has also contributed to higher claims in Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and Chhattisgarh.
 
According to PMFBY portal, the gross premium collected for kharif season in FY26 stood at ₹12,261.68 crore, nearly 15 per cent less than the premiums collected last year, while the sum insured increased by 26 per cent to ₹1.83 trillion.
 
Under the PMFBY, the sum insured for a farmer is determined by the scale of finance per hectare for a specific crop, as decided by the District-Level Technical Committee and pre-declared by the State-Level Committee. The total sum insured is calculated by multiplying the scale of finance by the area of the notified crop proposed to be insured.
 
Farmers pay relatively low premiums under the scheme — up to 2 per cent of the sum insured for kharif crops, up to 1.5 per cent for rabi crops, and up to 5 per cent for commercial and horticultural crops. The balance premium is shared equally by the Centre and state governments, except in the north-eastern states (from kharif 2020) and Himalayan states (from kharif 2023), where the sharing ratio is 90:10. Farmers are not required to pay any premium beyond these prescribed rates.
 
The PMFBY operational guidelines also provide for three alternative risk-transfer structures besides the standard model: cup-and-cap (80:110), cup-and-cap (60:130), and a profit-and-loss-sharing model. Under these structures, if claims remain below specified thresholds, a portion of the premium subsidy paid by the government is returned to the state treasury.
 
According to Rohit Boda, group managing director at the JB Boda Group, it is still early to arrive at a final picture of claims for the 2026 kharif season, but indicators so far point to a difficult year for the crop insurance market.
 
“Premium rates have also come down this year, which is another factor influencing the claims outlook. Overall, crop insurance premium rates have declined by approximately 36 per cent. The reduction has been particularly noticeable in states of Rajasthan, Maharashtra and Jharkhand, following the fresh tenders issued in 2026,” he said
 
According to Mohammad Faizan Huq, associate president and head of Agriculture, Parametric and A&H, and Reinsurance at Howden India, the overall premium collected under the PMFBY and the Restructured Weather Based Crop Insurance Scheme (RWBCIS) for the current kharif season is provisionally estimated at around ₹12,250 crore, more than 13 per cent lower than the previous season.
 
He added that according to early industry indications the all-India Kharif season's loss ratio (claims over premium) is expected to be well beyond 100 per cent. The loss ratio may vary with insurers depending upon their exposure in states where production losses are higher.
 
According to experts, lower rates were quoted by insurers in key states, including Maharashtra, Rajasthan and Karnataka. Insurers have also reduced the premium pool even as weather-related risks have increased, putting pressure on underwriting performance.
 
The claims experience is expected to be more challenging than last year, when the kharif season's claims ratio was around 90-100 per cent. The final claims liability for the current season, however, will depend on yield data emerging from field-level Crop Cutting Experiments (CCEs) and estimates generated through the YES-Tech system, or Yield Estimation System based on Technology.
 
Insurers are currently assessing crop losses, with the final claims numbers likely to emerge as state governments complete yield assessments and submit the necessary data. The wider coverage reflects increased participation in the scheme even as insurers brace for a difficult claims season, with the combination of lower premiums and higher weather-related losses likely to weigh on the industry's performance.

data.title: RBI cuts CRR maintenance requirement for banks back to 90% from Dec 1
data.description:
The Reserve Bank of India on Friday cut the minimum cash reserve ratio (CRR) maintenance requirement for banks back to 90 per cent, amid a decline in the surplus liquidity in the banking system. 
In October this year, the central bank had hiked the CRR maintenance requirement to 99 per cent from the earlier 90 per cent amid a liquidity surplus. 
"On the basis of an assessment of the current and evolving macroeconomic situation and liquidity conditions, it has been decided to reduce the minimum daily maintenance of the cash reserve ratio (CRR) from 99 per cent of the requirement to 90 per cent, effective from the fortnight beginning December 1, 2026," a central bank notification said. 
 
CRR is the quantum of deposits which banks have to park with the RBI. Banks do not earn any returns on the money set aside for CRR, and the ratio currently stands at 3 per cent of their deposits. 
The move comes days after the banking system liquidity turned to deficit for the first time in five months on the back of Goods and Services Tax outflows and the RBI's foreign exchange market interventions.

data.title: Rapido eyes deeper city expansion after Supreme Court's bike taxi ruling
data.description:
Ride-hailing platform Rapido is looking to deepen its presence in smaller cities and expand its footprint across the country following the Supreme Court's ruling on bike taxis.
 
The Bengaluru-based mobility platform, which currently operates in more than 400 cities, believes the ruling will help it engage with state governments and accelerate the adoption of bike taxis in markets where regulatory uncertainty has held back operations.
 
“With this regulatory clarity, we believe it is going to be easier for us to penetrate, expand much more deeper into the Bharat, deeper into the smaller towns. So, definitely, yes, we are going to go for expansion,” Rapido co-founder Pavan Guntupalli said in an interaction with Business Standard.
 
Last week, the Supreme Court dismissed the Karnataka government's appeal against the state’s high court judgment permitting motorcycle owners and aggregators to operate bike taxi services in the state, paving the way for their continued operation.
 
The company, however, has not set out a fresh numerical target for city additions following the ruling. Guntupalli said the platform had been awaiting regulatory clarity before committing to its next expansion targets. “The only thing that we have been looking for impetus is regulatory clarity, which we believe has now happened in as much as black and white,” he said.
 
Guntupalli said that 11 states had already put in place a framework for bike taxis, while some others were in the process of doing so. Safety concerns, he said, remained among the key reasons for regulatory hesitation.
 
The Supreme Court's ruling is expected to open up further discussions with state governments on safety requirements and regulatory frameworks, he said.
 
On the safety pain points, Guntupalli said the company has introduced background verification, training checks, round-the-clock customer support, and in-app alerts for speeding and rash driving. It also provides compulsory insurance for every ride, covering both drivers and customers, he added.
 
Guntupalli said that Rapido's expansion strategy is increasingly centred on addressing mobility gaps in smaller towns, where access to public transport remains limited. He added that the company's proposition in these markets is not merely about offering convenience but also about providing access to transportation.
 
“By taxi, especially in the smaller towns, we say we are providing access to transportation rather than convenience. It's not just convenience, it's actually access,” he said. The company believes its bike taxi model can find adoption across geographies with similar mobility requirements.
 
Rapido operates on a zero-commission model, under which drivers receive the entire customer payment after paying a fixed fee to the platform. The company said it was operationally profitable and had sufficient cash to fund its existing and future expansion plans, ruling out any immediate fundraising or initial public offering (IPO) plans.

data.title: TVS Motor forays into cargo tricycles with Armado, eyes overseas markets
data.description:
TVS Motor Company (TVSM), part of TVS VENU, announced the launch of TVS Armado on Friday, marking its foray into cargo tricycles with a one-tonne load capacity.
 
With this launch, TVS expands its commercial mobility portfolio with a tricycle designed to address the evolving needs of cargo transportation and first- and last-mile logistics.
 
“With TVS Armado, we become the first globally reputed OEM to enter the tricycle cargo segment, bringing an innovative, best-in-class product to the 1-tonne cargo mobility space,” said Peyman Kargar, president, international business, TVS Motor Company. By bringing together practical engineering, customer-focused design, and trusted after-sales support, TVS Armado is targeted at markets like Africa, Latin America, and Asean.
 
 
Recognising the needs of entrepreneurs, fleet owners, and delivery businesses, TVS Armado was developed with a customer-first approach, translating real-world operating requirements into a dependable mobility solution designed to keep businesses moving day in, day out.
 
"First- and last-mile logistics is critical to businesses and communities, and TVS Armado is designed around the real needs of customers and business owners, combining load-carrying capability, world-class reliability and durability with the practicality required for everyday commercial use," Kargar said.
 
The TVS Armado is powered by a robust 200 cc oil-cooled engine, delivering 10.6 kW of maximum power at 7,500 rpm and 15.5 Nm of peak torque at 5,000 rpm, paired with a five-speed manual transmission. Designed for demanding commercial mobility solutions, it features a 16-litre fuel tank to support extended operating hours.
 
Its two-metre-long cargo bed offers a vast loading area with a payload capacity of up to one tonne, enabling businesses to transport a wide range of goods efficiently. The large cargo bed, along with 230 mm of ground clearance and strong leaf spring suspension, is designed to support operations across varied road conditions, including urban, suburban, and rural routes.
 
The first-in-industry oil-cooled engine is designed to offer a practical balance of durability and ease of maintenance, backed by the best-in-category warranty terms, which reinforce customer confidence in long-term ownership.
 
"As we build our commercial mobility portfolio globally, TVS Armado reflects our ambition to create solutions that deliver tangible business value and contribute to the growth of communities," he added.
 
With TVS Armado, TVS Motor Company builds on its experience in commercial mobility to address the evolving needs of cargo transportation. "TVS Armado aims to be a reliable business partner for those who work relentlessly to build a better future, in line with TVS Motor’s vision of transforming the quality of life of people across the world by providing mobility solutions that are exciting, responsible, sustainable and safe,” he said.

data.title: Ramayana expands global footprint, becomes No. 1 Indian film in 27 nations
data.description:
Nitesh Tiwari's Ramayana: Rise of a Legend has become the highest-grossing Indian film of all time in 27 countries, setting box office records across North America, Europe, Southeast Asia and parts of Africa.
 
This achievement comes as the film's total global collection surpassed Rs 1,777 crore within 22 days. The movie premiered in cinemas globally on November 5, available in Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, and Malayalam.

Ramayana worldwide box office update

Starring Ranbir Kapoor and Yash, Ramayana has seen its daily domestic collections decline after an impressive opening run, during which it earned over Rs 100 crore worldwide for seven consecutive days. Its daily earnings in India have now fallen below Rs 10 crore net.
 
 
However, globally, it experienced a boost in its third week, once again making over $1 million per day on Thursday, which marked its 22nd day in cinemas. This upward trend has carried Ramayana’s domestic earnings to ₹992 crore net (₹1185 crore gross). 
 
Internationally, Ramayana improved significantly after an unimpressive start. It has performed well in the United States and in smaller markets like Thailand, Vietnam, and Nepal, amassing over $64 million internationally in 22 days. 
 
Consequently, Ramayana’s total earnings have reached ₹1777 crore globally. It holds the title of the fourth-highest-grossing film in Indian cinema history. 
ALSO READ: Samay Raina makes YouTube history with 1 million paid channel members

Ramayana breaks global records

The makers of Ramayana revealed on Thursday that the Nitesh Tiwari-directed movie has achieved the status of ‘#1 Indian film of all time’ in 27 nations. 
 
This list of countries where Ramayana stands as the top-grossing Indian film comprises the US, the UK, Indonesia, and Thailand, along with emerging markets such as Vietnam, Cambodia, and numerous other European nations. 
 
The film has garnered substantial acclaim in Southeast Asia, particularly in countries like Cambodia and Singapore, where the epic has a strong following. With Sony Pictures providing a broad release, it has also unlocked new opportunities for Bollywood in countries such as Slovakia, Ukraine, Latvia, Georgia, Armenia, and various Caribbean locations. 
ALSO READ: Hanuman Ansh OTT release: When and where to watch spiritual biopic online?

All about Ramayana

Directed by Nitesh Tiwari, Ramayana represents the first installment of a 2-part series. The cast includes Ranbir Kapoor portraying Lord Rama, Sai Pallavi playing Sita, Yash as Ravana, and Ravie Dubey as Lakshman. 
 
With production handled by Namit Malhotra and Yash, Ramayana is being hailed as the costliest Indian film ever produced. The second part is set to be released in 2028. 
ALSO READ: Ye Prem Mol Liya box office collection: Film records slow opening on day 1

data.title: High energy prices cost India an extra ₹6-7 trn annually: Tarun Kapoor
data.description:
India's high oil and gas import dependence, coupled with high global energy prices, is costing the country between ₹6 lakh crore and ₹7 lakh crore extra annually, and the solution lies in citizens cutting avoidable fuel consumption, Tarun Kapoor, adviser to Prime Minister Narendra Modi in the Prime Minister's Office (PMO), said today.
 
Speaking at a Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) event on energy security, he said the impact of this large dependence on imports is being felt across the economy, including in fuel prices, freight rates, and overall inflation.
 
"Large dependence on imports has shown that we are so vulnerable that we may be caught in a tight situation and it can be disastrous for the country. Just this high price of crude and natural gas is costing us at least ₹6-7 lakh crore extra every year," Kapoor said.
 
 
India imported over 293 million tonnes (MT) of crude oil and petroleum products last financial year (2025-26) at a cost of over ₹13 lakh crore, according to Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC) data. In the first seven months of the current financial year, the country spent ₹11.4 lakh crore to import 161 MT of crude oil and products.
 
"The government has so far absorbed quite a bit of the increase in price which should have been passed on to the customers. The oil companies have very graciously absorbed a part of that increase but had it all been passed on to the consumers, as has been done in most of the countries like US or Europe, the impact on all consumer goods and supplies would have been disastrous," Kapoor said.
 
He added that countries like China have been able to overcome the shock by building huge energy storage capacity, but that solution has its limits, as storage capacity cannot be built for two-three years.
 
"Storage can be built at best for 90 days or a little more but that also helps because if even a part of your requirement comes from what your stored, you at least know when to buy or play with the market. We are like a person who goes every day to the market to buy his ration and comes back and eats it. This is because we have very little storage," Kapoor said.
 
He also said that given the huge energy consumption of the country, strategies like diversification of oil supplies, looking for alternative sources, and entering into long-term contracts, too, have limited gains. He said it is more important that citizens cut avoidable consumption, reiterating Prime Minister Narendra Modi's recent call.
 
Modi had recently urged citizens to cut fuel, gold, and foreign-linked consumption to conserve foreign exchange reserves and ease import pressures amid the West Asia and Strait of Hormuz crisis.
 
"Citizens can do that. What we have seen is that initially when the PM gave the call, there was a bit of a reduction but the economy is growing," Kapoor said, adding that the last few months have witnessed a more-than-normal increase in energy consumption due to economic growth.
 
He added that the country needs dedicated policy intervention to ramp up the pace of the shift towards electric trucks, a cost-effective mode of transport.

data.title: Sebi clarifies no change proposed to managing director age limit at MIIs
data.description:
The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) on Friday clarified that its consultation paper on strengthening governance of market infrastructure institutions (MIIs) does not propose any change to the maximum age limit of 65 years for their managing directors (MDs). MIIs include stock exchanges, depositories, and clearing corporations. The regulator said that the proposals floated on November 20 regarding MDs concern only their term and tenure within a single MII and across MIIs. Incumbent public interest directors, MDs, and executive directors would continue till the end of their ongoing terms.
 
Sebi has proposed that a single term for a managing director (MD) would not exceed five years, with a maximum of two terms and eight years in one MII.
 
 
The proposed changes include lower age and term limits for public interest directors (PIDs), a 12-year cap on the combined tenure of managing directors across MIIs, and a board seat for the Association of Mutual Funds in India’s (Amfi’s) chief executive at the repo clearing corporation.
 
The regulator has proposed cutting the maximum age of PIDs from 75 to 70 years and the cap on terms from three to two. A PID would serve two terms of three years each across MIIs.
 
The regulator said the role is quasi-regulatory and more demanding than that of an ordinary non-executive director, and that a narrow pool of individuals can circulate between MIIs. 
Sebi allows FPIs to trade in physically settled non-agri commodity derivatives
 
The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) on Friday announced that it would allow foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) to participate in physically settled non-agricultural commodity derivatives, expanding their access beyond cash-settled contracts. The move, aimed at deepening institutional participation and liquidity, will come into effect from June 1, 2027. FPIs will have to square off or roll over positions before the tender or staggered delivery period. If they fail to do so, open positions will automatically devolve upon a designated trading member or trading-cum-clearing member under a safeguard mechanism.

data.title: Vivo X500 Pro Max first impressions: Premium phone built around photography
data.description:
The Vivo X500 Pro Max is not a smartphone that blends into the crowd. From its large circular camera module to its sizeable display, the device makes its intentions clear. It is designed for users who place photography high on their list of priorities, and Vivo has gone a step further by offering optional teleconverter attachments to extend its imaging capabilities. Having spent some time with the device, its design, in-hand feel and display have made a good first impression.
 
Starting with the design, the Vivo X500 Pro Max retains the circular camera arrangement seen on its predecessor. However, the company has made some changes to the rear panel. The upper portion of the glass back, which houses the camera module, is slightly raised and slopes gently into the rest of the panel. This gives the phone a distinctive appearance without making the camera housing feel like an entirely separate component.
 
 
The aluminium frame adds to the construction, while the glass back has a smooth finish with a subtle pattern. It does attract fingerprints, though. The phone is available in Apex Orange and Eternal Black colour options, with different finishes on the rear panel.
ALSO READ: Vivo X500 series launched in India: Check specs, price details, and more
Despite its sizeable camera hardware, the X500 Pro Max measures between 7.95mm and 8.12mm in thickness, depending on the colour variant, and weighs 225g or 229g. It is not a lightweight smartphone, but the weight distribution makes it reasonably comfortable to hold. The index finger naturally rests below the camera module, which also helps when holding the phone in landscape orientation for photography. However, its large footprint means two-handed operation is often more convenient.
 
The camera system is where Vivo wants the X500 Pro Max to distinguish itself. The phone features a 50MP primary camera, a 50MP ultra-wide camera and a 200MP ZEISS APO telephoto camera. The latter has an 85mm equivalent focal length and is the centrepiece of the setup.
 
Vivo is also offering optional teleconverter attachments to extend the phone's photography capabilities. The range includes a 200mm equivalent ZEISS Telephoto Extender Gen 2 and a 400mm equivalent Gen 2 Ultra. There is also an Imaging Grip Kit with a physical shutter button and zoom dial. Together, these accessories make the phone resemble a compact camera setup and are aimed at users interested in wildlife and long-distance photography.
 
Moving to the front, the X500 Pro Max features a 6.85-inch 2K ZEISS Master Color AMOLED display with a 144Hz refresh rate. The panel has narrow, symmetrical bezels and a flat design, while a small punch-hole houses the front camera. The screen looks sharp, with deep blacks and vibrant colours.
ALSO READ: GTA 6 India launch: First impressions, prices, editions and download size
The LTPO panel can dynamically switch its refresh rate between 1Hz and 144Hz, depending on the content. Vivo claims peak brightness of up to 5,000 nits, while the high-brightness mode is rated at 2,000 nits. The display also supports Dolby Vision and HDR10+, while an ultrasonic fingerprint sensor is embedded underneath.
 
The Vivo X500 Pro Max makes a good first impression with its design, in-hand feel and AMOLED display. The teleconverter attachments also give it a different proposition from conventional flagship smartphones. However, their usefulness and the extent to which they improve the photography experience need closer examination.
 
There is still more to assess, including camera performance across different conditions, processing capabilities, software and battery life. The full review of the Vivo X500 Pro Max will be out soon.

Vivo X500 Pro Max: Price and availability

The smartphone is available for pre-booking in India, with open sales scheduled to begin on December 3.
  • 12GB RAM + 256GB storage: Rs 164,999
  • 12GB RAM + 512GB storage: Rs 179,999
Accessories available for separate purchase:
  • 400 mm Equivalent vivo ZEISS Telephoto Extender Gen 2 Ultra: Rs 27,999
  • 200 mm Equivalent vivo ZEISS Telephoto Extender Gen 2: Rs 15,999
  • Imaging Grip Kit: Rs 11,999
  • Phone Strap: Rs 2,699
  • Magnetic Case: Rs 1,499 (X500 Pro Max and X500 Pro)
Customers can also get the 12GB RAM + 512GB storage variant of the Vivo X500 Pro Max with the Photography Kit at Rs 229,999. It includes the smartphone, a 200mm equivalent ZEISS Telephoto Extender Gen 2, a 400mm equivalent ZEISS Telephoto Extender Gen 2 Ultra and a shoulder strap.

data.title: Collegium favours a 'particular section' over merit, diversity: Ex-CJI
data.description:
Former Chief Justice of India BR Gavai on Friday wrote to President Droupadi Murmu seeking her intervention in judicial appointments and transfers. He alleged that recent Collegium recommendations favour candidates from "one particular section of the society", at the expense of merit, diversity and inclusivity.
 
In a three-page letter, Gavai alleged that candidates from one section of society were being favoured for elevation to the higher judiciary, while Scheduled Castes (SCs), Scheduled Tribes (STs), Other Backward Classes (OBCs), minorities, women and other communities were being excluded.
 
"I am constrained to voice my dissent and disappointment," Gavai wrote, alleging that recent appointments and transfers were being made in disregard of diversity, inclusion and merit.
 
 
The letter was addressed to President Murmu and marked to Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal.

Gavai questions representation in higher judiciary

Gavai said a community accounting for less than 5 per cent of India's population had secured more than 40 per cent representation in the Supreme Court in the recent past.
 
He also referred to data presented by Union Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal in the Rajya Sabha in March 2025.
 
According to the data, of the 715 high court judges appointed since 2018, 22 belonged to the Scheduled Castes (SCs), 16 to the Scheduled Tribes (STs), 89 to the Other Backward Classes (OBCs) and 37 to minority communities. Together, these four categories accounted for 164 appointments, or around 23 per cent of the total.
 
Gavai said the representation of different sections of society had been considered during his tenure in the Collegium.
 
In the letter, he wrote: "When I was a part of the collegium and was Chief Justice of India, I always followed the principles of diversity and inclusion."
 
He added that adequate representation was ensured for SCs, STs, OBCs, minorities and women while considering candidates for elevation to the high courts and the Supreme Court.
 
However, he alleged that recent recommendations ignored these principles. "In the recent past disturbing events have unfolded, showing complete disregard for the principles of merit and inclusivity," he wrote.

Gavai questions recent transfers and appointments

The former CJI also raised concerns over the transfer of high court judges and subsequent recommendations for their elevation.
 
He referred to an instance in which a chief justice was transferred from one high court to a smaller high court and was subsequently recommended for appointment as the chief justice of a prominent high court.
 
Gavai alleged that another meritorious and hardworking chief justice was transferred to a smaller high court to accommodate the appointment.
 
He said he had been part of the Collegium that recommended the first chief justice's transfer and later headed the Collegium when the subsequent transfer recommendation was made.
 
"I am aware of the factors that prevailed at the relevant time with the collegium for recommending such an appointment/transfer. However, on account of propriety and judicial disciple I refrain from divulging these reasons," he wrote.
 
Citing another instance, Gavai alleged that a judge who had been transferred from his parent high court to another high court on punitive considerations was subsequently appointed chief justice of a large and prominent high court.
 
"In another instance, a judge was transferred from his parent high court to another high court on punitive consideration and was subsequently rewarded by appointment as chief justice of a large and a prominent high court," the letter read.

Gavai urges President to intervene

Gavai also questioned whether the Collegium's primacy in judicial appointments could place it beyond accountability.
 
Referring to Article 124(2) of the Constitution, which provides for the appointment of Supreme Court judges by the President, he argued that the President's constitutional responsibilities remained relevant to the process.
 
He said the Collegium's recommendations being treated as decisive under judicial convention did not make the body unaccountable or absolve the President of her constitutional duties.
 
Gavai also said the executive and Parliament were stakeholders in judicial appointments and transfers. He referred to instances in which the government and legislature had requested the Collegium and high courts to consider suitable candidates from marginalised communities to improve representation.
 
He urged President Murmu to intervene, as she deemed appropriate, and remind all stakeholders of their constitutional responsibilities towards ensuring equal representation in the higher judiciary.

data.title: Canada Express Entry: 600 invited for PR in first STEM draw since 2024
data.description:
Canada on Thursday resumed category-based Express Entry draws for science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) occupations after a gap of more than 31 months, issuing 600 invitations to apply (ITAs) for permanent residency.
 
Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) set the minimum Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score at 547 for the draw. Candidates needed eligible work experience in one of 11 occupations to qualify.
 
This was the third Express Entry draw in November. It followed a Provincial Nominee Program draw on November 23, which issued 1,999 invitations, and a Canadian Experience Class (CEC) draw earlier in the month.
 

How does Canada's Express Entry system work?

 
Express Entry is Canada's online system for managing applications for permanent residence under three federal economic immigration programmes:
  
Federal Skilled Worker Program
Federal Skilled Trades Program
Canadian Experience Class
 
Candidates create an online profile and receive a CRS score based on factors such as age, education, work experience and language proficiency. IRCC conducts regular draws and invites candidates who meet the applicable score and category requirements to apply for permanent residence.
 

Canada Express Entry: Details of the November 26 STEM draw

 
The November 26 draw was conducted at 12:52 UTC. Its key details were:
 
Draw type: Category-based selection – STEM occupations
Invitations issued: 600
Minimum CRS score: 547
Rank required: 600 or higher
Tie-breaking date: December 2, 2025, at 16:52:51 UTC
 
The tie-breaking rule applies to candidates with the minimum CRS score of 547. Those who submitted their Express Entry profiles before the specified date and time were given priority over candidates with the same score who submitted their profiles later.
 

Why is this STEM draw important?

 
IRCC had not conducted a STEM-specific Express Entry draw since April 11, 2024, when it issued 4,500 invitations with a minimum CRS score of 491.
 
Earlier STEM draws included:
 
December 2023: 5,900 invitations, with a CRS cutoff of 481.
July 2023: 500 invitations, with a CRS cutoff of 486.
 
The November 26 draw differs from these earlier rounds in three ways.
 
First, its CRS cutoff of 547 is considerably higher than the previous STEM draw thresholds. Second, the number of invitations has fallen to 600, compared with thousands in the 2023 and 2024 rounds.
 
Third, the eligible occupation list has been reduced from 24 NOC codes to 11 under the revised Express Entry categories announced in February 2026.
 

Which 11 occupations qualify for the STEM draw?

 
The following occupations under Canada's National Occupational Classification (NOC) 2021 system were eligible for the November 26 selection round:
 
1. Architecture and science managers (TEER 0)
2. Cybersecurity specialists (TEER 1)
3. Civil engineers (TEER 1)
4. Mechanical engineers (TEER 1)
5. Electrical and electronics engineers (TEER 1)
6. Industrial and manufacturing engineers (TEER 1)
7. Geological engineers (TEER 1)
8. Civil engineering technologists and technicians (TEER 2)
9. Mechanical engineering technologists and technicians (TEER 2)
10. Electrical and electronics engineering technologists and technicians (TEER 2)
11. Insurance agents and brokers (TEER 3)
 
Several technology occupations, including software developers (NOC 21232), software engineers (NOC 21231), data scientists (NOC 21211) and web developers (NOC 21234), are no longer included in the revised list. 
ALSO READ: Canada could admit 662k permanent residents in 2027, 74% above target: RBC
 

What are the eligibility requirements for STEM candidates?

 
Under the 2026 category-based selection framework, candidates must have at least 12 months of cumulative work experience in an eligible occupation within the previous three years.
 
The experience can be acquired in Canada or abroad and does not need to be continuous. It must meet IRCC's requirements for full-time work or its equivalent in part-time employment.
 
This is a change from the previous six-month work experience requirement and narrows the pool of candidates eligible for STEM-specific draws.
 

What should candidates do after receiving an ITA?

 
Candidates invited in the November 26 draw have 60 days from the date of invitation to submit a complete application for permanent residence.
 
They should:
 
1. Check their eligibility: Verify that their work experience matches one of the 11 eligible NOC occupations. Job duties, rather than job titles alone, determine the appropriate NOC classification.
2. Prepare supporting documents: These include valid language test results, an Educational Credential Assessment (ECA), employment reference letters, police clearance certificates and medical examination documents, as applicable.
3. Meet the deadline: Submit the complete permanent residence application within 60 days of receiving the ITA. Failure to meet the deadline means the invitation expires.
4. Update relevant information: Disclose changes in employment, education, language scores or other circumstances that could affect CRS scores or eligibility.
 
An invitation to apply does not guarantee permanent residence. IRCC assesses the supporting documents and verifies that applicants meet the programme's eligibility requirements before making a final decision. 
ALSO READ: 9.25 lakh Indians became OECD citizens in five years, up 40%: Report
